claim: WHO estimates 684,000 fatal falls and 37.3 million falls requiring medical attention each year, with over 80% of fall-related fatalities in low- and middle-income countries and the highest death rates among adults over 60.
method: Reviewed the WHO fact sheet key facts, problem definition, global burden, age pattern, DALY context, exclusions, and listed prevention strategies.
limitations: The page reports global estimates and does not provide a current older-adult incidence denominator for a named LMIC district.
The fall-related death and non-fatal injury estimates use WHO Global Health Estimates and exclude specified assault, self-harm, transport, fire, water, and machinery circumstances.
The 37.3-million medically attended figure is not a count of unique older adults and cannot be used to infer rehabilitation need or treatment effectiveness.
The fact sheet does not establish that any listed prevention strategy reduces mortality or disability in a particular setting.

claim: WHO's Step Safely technical package organizes fall-prevention and management evidence for children and adolescents, workers, community-dwelling older people, older people in residential care, and older people receiving hospital care.

source.title: Step safely: strategies for preventing and managing falls across the life-course

method: Reviewed the WHO package description, publication date, named population groups, examples of prevention strategies, and description of the commissioned evidence-synthesis process.
limitations: The package is a synthesis and technical resource, not a country implementation evaluation or local effect estimate.
Evidence quality and transferability differ by population group, intervention, health system, and setting; the package does not authorize a universal programme.
The page does not establish that LMIC facilities can deliver every recommended component or sustain follow-up.
Any clinical or community intervention use requires local domain, safeguarding, feasibility, and replication review.

claim: WHO's global report on falls prevention in older age reports that approximately 28–35% of people aged 65 years and over fall each year, increasing to 32–42% among people over 70, and links allocation to better knowledge of scale, nature, and intervention effectiveness.

source.title: WHO global report on falls prevention in older age

method: Reviewed the WHO report overview for the age-specific fall estimates, rationale for prevention, resource-targeting requirement, framework, and stated scope.
limitations: The report is historical and does not provide current country- or district-specific estimates.
The reported ranges are not a substitute for a compatible LMIC sampling frame, local fall definition, recurrence rule, or injury threshold.
The report does not establish current intervention effect sizes, workforce feasibility, or post-fall rehabilitation capacity.
The source is a global planning report and cannot justify individual assessment or treatment decisions.

claim: A nationally representative WHO SAGE Wave 1 analysis of adults aged 50 years and older in China, Ghana, India, Mexico, the Russian Federation, and South Africa reported a 4.0% pooled prevalence of self-reported past-year fall-related injury and an association with disability.

source.title: Prevalence, risk factors and disability associated with fall-related injury in older adults in low- and middle-income countries: results from the WHO Study on global AGEing and adult health (SAGE)

method: Reviewed the peer-reviewed article abstract and methods for the six-country SAGE sampling frame, age threshold, fall-related injury definition, self-reported past-year window, WHODAS disability measure, and regression analysis.
limitations: The data are from SAGE Wave 1 and largely reflect 2007–2010 collection periods, so they are not current surveillance.
The study includes adults aged 50 years and older, not only adults aged 60 years and older, and the pooled estimate should not be relabelled as an older-old or district rate.
Fall-related injury and disability are self-reported and cross-sectional; the association is not evidence of causation or intervention effect.
National representativeness within six countries does not establish comparability for other LMICs or for facility-based care pathways.

claim: A prospective injury-registry study across 23 health facilities in Malawi and Tanzania recorded 93,178 trauma patients, including 44,609 with fall-related complaints; median arrival time was 10 hours and 3,275 fall patients had potentially serious injuries in the registry population.

source.title: Fall injuries in Sub-Saharan Africa: analysis of prospective injury registry from 23 health facilities in Malawi and Tanzania

method: Reviewed the article abstract and methods for the number and type of facilities, registry periods, trauma denominator, fall-complaint count, arrival-time definition, serious-injury definition, and facility selection.
limitations: The registry covers selected facilities along highway and emergency-service corridors and is not a population incidence denominator.
The reported arrival interval includes both travel time and time before deciding to seek care, so it cannot be treated as prehospital transport time alone.
The registry population is predominantly young and male; it does not isolate older-adult prevention or functional recovery.
The observational design and differing registry emphasis between Malawi and Tanzania do not identify a causal effect of emergency or prevention interventions.

claim: The FAMILY cluster randomized clinical trial evaluated a primary-care-integrated fall-prevention programme in 128 rural Chinese villages, randomized 2,610 adults aged 60 years and older, and reported at least one self-reported fall in 29.7% of intervention participants versus 38.3% of controls over 12 months.

source.title: A Fall Prevention Program Integrated in Primary Health Care for Older People in Rural China: The FAMILY Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial

method: Reviewed the PubMed abstract and linked full text for cluster count, eligibility, randomization, intervention components, follow-up, primary outcome, functional measures, attrition before randomization, and reported odds ratio.
limitations: The trial was conducted in four rural Chinese provinces within a specific primary-care system and cannot establish transportability to other LMICs.
The primary fall outcome was self-reported and collected quarterly with a calendar; it is not a blinded clinical or population surveillance measure.

Eligibility excluded people unable to walk without assistance, some neurodegenerative conditions, short life expectancy, and speech or hearing limitations, limiting generalizability to higher-risk groups.
The trial estimates one bundled intervention effect and does not show which component caused the result or establish mortality, fracture, hospitalization, or long-term functional benefit.

claim: WHO's Data Set for Injury provides a standardized set of core and extended variables for systematic injury-care documentation and quality improvement, intended to support aggregation and comparison across hospitals, regions, and countries.
method: Reviewed the WHO publication overview for the dataset's purpose, stakeholder consultation, core and extended element structure, clinical-form linkage, and intended comparison grain.
limitations: The dataset is designed for injury-care documentation and does not estimate unobserved community falls or population incidence.
A standardized variable list does not ensure complete reporting, compatible implementation, reliable timestamps, or representative facility coverage.
The source does not provide older-adult fall-specific functional follow-up, prevention exposure, home hazards, or rehabilitation completion by itself.
Clinical data collection requires local governance, qualified staff, privacy safeguards, and a reviewed use case.

claim: WHO's Clinical Registry provides a web and Android platform for structured emergency and injury data collection, with a WHO Data Set for Injury of 41 core and 27 extended elements and an emergency-care dataset that includes prehospital time metrics.
method: Reviewed the WHO registry page for platform purpose, offline and Android operation, clinical modules, Data Set for Injury element counts, emergency-care prehospital fields, and quality-improvement use.
limitations: The registry is a facility-based platform and cannot establish population incidence, community fall exposure, or people who never seek care.
Platform availability does not prove local implementation, data completeness, staff training, referral closure, rehabilitation follow-up, or patient consent.
The injury elements are not a complete older-adult fall-prevention or functional-recovery protocol and require country adaptation.
Use of person-level clinical data requires lawful governance, privacy protection, qualified clinical ownership, and an explicit non-use boundary.
